claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has a homogeneous fcc matrix.
The alloying elements are well distributed in the initial state.
The as-printed alloy has no pre-formed surface oxide scale.
Elevated-temperature degradation of this alloy is governed by formation and integrity of a duplex oxide scale.
Oxidizing exposure produces a coherent inner oxide layer enriched in Cr and Ti.
A less-protective and less-adherent outer oxide layer forms secondarily during oxidizing exposure.
The high oxygen affinity of Cr and Ti drives their surface segregation and preferential oxidation.
The inner Cr/Ti-rich oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier that limits oxygen ingress and alloy-element transport.
Barrier action by the inner oxide slows further oxidation and protects the underlying fcc matrix.
Reducing H2/CO-rich exposure inhibits or slows formation of the protective inner oxide layer.
Inhibition of the inner oxide under reducing conditions causes less stable passivation and faster surface degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will preserve mechanical integrity better than reducing exposure.
Reducing exposure will produce a less-protective or discontinuous oxide scale.
Reducing exposure will cause greater scale spallation or greater surface microstructural damage than oxidizing exposure.
Protection by the inner oxide accounts for retention of strength and fatigue performance during moderate oxidation.
The proposed mechanism is intended to apply between 700°C and 1000°C over exposures ranging from hours to hundreds of hours.
Extreme temperatures or exceedingly long exposures may activate additional degradation mechanisms.
